problem: Model-free RL needs huge amounts of interaction, which is too costly on real robots, and training on limited real experience overfits (learned visual features, fixed observations), so policies fail to transfer to day-to-day environment variation.
motivation: Mobile robots have limited battery and human supervision but spare offline compute. The paper turns one real traversal into a virtual environment the agent can replay interactively, and asks whether the resulting policy transfers zero-shot to a second traversal recorded under natural variation.
key_idea: Build a pose-graph world model from a single real traversal, train a bootstrapped Q-learning agent in it with a frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 encoder and stochastic position/orientation observation sampling, and transfer to a validation traversal with no fine-tuning.
insight: Overfitting to the single traversal is the main obstacle, and it is countered by injecting observation noise and using frozen pre-trained features. Per the Fig. 5 ablations, stochastic observations give near-optimal Rmin and improve the validation/training ratio, and pre-trained features transfer better than a from-scratch encoder. Bootstrapped Q-learning beats A2C and n-step Q-learning, plausibly because diverse random priors find forward-biased trajectories.
method: Interactive replay: a single traversal is aligned (with minimal human loop closing) into a pose graph with snapshots every 10 cm; the agent turns 90° or moves forward between nodes, giving a virtual environment.
Validation environment: a second traversal on a different day, in a different order, is aligned to the training graph nodes via laser localization plus a 360° camera (or manual annotation).
Rich visual encoding: a frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 (2048-d pre-final layer) is applied to four 90° views, concatenated to 8192-d, and precomputed for speed.
Stochastic observations: at each state the observation is sampled from images recorded 'in between' nodes, with position variance 5 cm and orientation variance 5°.
Bootstrapped Q-learning: double dueling n-step Q-learning with a shared LSTM and NQ=10 heads (pQ=0.5, one head chosen per episode), run with Nw=64 parallel workers.
Task and reward: a fixed goal (reward 1.0) plus 10 random sub-goals (0.1 each), respawn on reaching the goal, Tmax=3000, 300M virtual frames; the goal is not visible in images.

setting.backbone: Frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 encoder + LSTM + 10-head bootstrapped dueling Q-network (trained with RL)
setting.training_data: One real traversal of an office (572-node pose graph), 300M frames of virtual replay experience; ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet
setting.observation: 360° camera split into four 90° RGB views, encoded as an 8192-d ResNet-50 feature vector
setting.action_space: discrete {turn_left, turn_right, move_forward}, 90° turns and 10 cm steps between graph nodes
setting.simulator: Custom pose-graph replay environment built from real recorded imagery (Pioneer 3DX robot data); no standard simulator
setting.privileged: Pose graph of the environment from the traversal (human-aligned loop closures) used for training; fixed goal location; no privileged information at test time beyond the learned policy

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (Fig. 5, Rmin curves and Rrelative); no numeric tables. Text states only that an optimal agent would achieve Rmin ≥ 13 and that stochastic agents reach nearly optimal Rmin.
results: Bootstrapped Q-learning significantly outperforms A2C and n-step Q-learning, which fail to reliably solve the task. Stochastic observations bring the worst-case reward Rmin near the optimal-planner level and improve transfer to the validation traversal. Pre-trained visual features also improve validation performance and transfer ratio over a from-scratch encoder.
limitations: Open-loop evaluation only, in the recorded pose graph; no closed-loop real-robot deployment, and a low-level motion controller is still needed for the coarse discrete actions.
Single fixed goal in one known environment, discretized to 90° turns; the training graph needs human alignment, and there are no numeric tables (results only in plots).
builds_on: Learning to Navigate in Complex Environments
compares_to: random walk with near-optimal action prior
